_contract: Authored by Tasklet 2026-08-16 natively to contract v3, mirroring the Dubai v3 public-partners gold master per the international addendum (Bahrain run — Public Transport page, authority audience: Ministry of Transportation & Telecommunications + BTEA). Sources: bahrain/AUTHORITY-MAP-BAHRAIN.md + SPEED-RULES-BAHRAIN.md + NODES-BAHRAIN.md + DEMAND-POOLS-BAHRAIN.md + FARE-BENCHMARKS-BAHRAIN.md + REVENUE-INPUTS-BAHRAIN.md + CREW-COST-BENCHMARKS-BAHRAIN.md. CONTRACT v3: only `title` (<=6 words), `value`/figures, `note` (<=140 chars, partner-clean plain English), `status` (enum: market_priced | modeled | upside), and `fn` (footnote key) render — plus verbatim copy fields (headline/subline/lead/body/chips/cards). Underscore-prefixed fields NEVER reach the DOM. null/missing = render nothing. Footnotes render ONCE in a single 'Notes & assumptions' section above the contact form; a footnote's source_url may render as a small domain chip, never as a naked URL in body copy. Posture per AUTHORITY-MAP-BAHRAIN.md: Enable-led dual — the ministry regulates and licenses, operators run; the Kingdom has already put a six-station water-taxi service and an international ferry gateway in service, so the page leads with Bahrain's own momentum and the ask is 'extend the mode you already chose'. Domestic corridors only — cross-border Eastern Province/Qatar links appear as one roadmap line with no economics. No counterparty identities, no program or fleet commitments, no launch dates, no service-start years for any Navier service. The existing operator is described generically as 'Bahrain's water-taxi service' per the disclosure rails — no operator brand renders.

fn1.text: Bahrain's water-taxi service operates six stations on the Manama–Muharraq shore, with published fares of BHD 0.8 standard and BHD 1.5 VIP per station and day passes at BHD 2.5–5, on an air-conditioned 28-seat vessel.

fn2.text: Visitor figures from Bahrain's official open-data portal: 15.18 million inbound visitors in 2025, and arrivals by sea of 205,000 in 2024 — roughly three times the 69,000 of 2023.

fn3.text: King Fahd Causeway traffic per Saudi Arabia's official road-transport statistics for 2024, as reported: roughly 32.9 million passengers in the year — about half of all Saudi land-border traffic.

fn4.text: Ports, harbours, piers and private jetties are regulated by the Ministry of Transportation and Telecommunications under the Kingdom's ports and marine navigation law; vessels under 150 gross tonnes register under the small-ship law, with master and navigation licences issued by the ministry. Navigation conduct is set through licence conditions and Coast Guard notices — no allowance beyond that framework is assumed anywhere on this page.

fn5.text: All trip times use conservative speed assumptions in marinas, channels and harbours, with open-water segments at the vessel's service speed. Service hours are modeled 06:00–18:00; evening extension is subject to Coast Guard authorization.

fn6.text: Race-weekend attendance as published by the circuit: about 105,000 across the 2025 Formula 1 weekend, with 55% international visitors.

fn7.text: A scheduled international passenger ferry operates between Qatar and Sa'ada Marina, about 70–80 minutes each way, per consistent public reporting.

fn8.text: The Kingdom's net-zero 2060 target, with an interim reduction of about 30% by 2035, as announced at COP26 and filed with the UNFCCC.

copy.headline: Bahrain has already chosen the water.
copy.subline: A fast, zero-emission foiling tier across Manama, Muharraq, Amwaj and the southern islands — built on stations, marinas and jetties that already exist, financed by private capital, extending the water-taxi network the Kingdom already runs.

copy.lead: This Kingdom is not waiting to be convinced about water transport. A six-station water-taxi service is running on the Manama–Muharraq shore, a scheduled international passenger ferry now calls at Sa'ada Marina, and arrivals by sea tripled in a single year.
copy.support: A zero-emission foiling tier is additive reach, speed and range for a mode Bahrain has already chosen — on landings that already exist, at zero terminal cost to the Kingdom.

plans.note: Six stations across the Manama–Muharraq shore with published fares — the Kingdom has already put the mode in service.
A scheduled passenger ferry now links Sa'ada Marina with Qatar — marine passenger operations at gateway scale are licensed here.
Arrivals by sea went from 69,000 to 205,000 in a year, on official data — the water mode is growing before any new capacity.
The Kingdom's net-zero 2060 target and ~30% cut by 2035 are stated policy — a zero-emission tier maps directly onto them.

copy.headline: Every stop is an existing landing. No terminals to build.
copy.body: Zero terminal capital cost for the Kingdom. Service can start at live water-taxi stations, operating marinas and resort jetties — all fourteen stops on this network are existing landings today.

copy.framing: One conversation, not two. Bahrain regulates and licenses marine transport through one ministry, and the Kingdom has already shown its model on this water: government enables, operators run. The posture here is extension — more reach, more speed, more range for the mode Bahrain has already chosen.
copy.enable_track: License the routes, vessels and landings under the existing small-vessel and port framework. Private capital finances the vessels; the ask is licensing and access, not money.
copy.operate_track: Where the Kingdom prefers procurement, the foiling tier can be concessioned the way today's water-taxi service runs — a franchise on the ministry's terms, with fares slotted above the existing public water-taxi ladder.

operate_proof_points.body: Ministry of Transportation & Telecommunications — Ports & Maritime Affairs
operate_proof_points.proof: Regulates every port, harbour, pier and private jetty in the Kingdom, licenses operators, registers vessels under 150 gross tonnes, and issues master and navigation licences — one ministry, one licensing conversation.
Six live stations, published fares and an air-conditioned passenger vessel — the enable-and-operate model is already working on exactly this water.
Sa'ada Marina hosts a scheduled international passenger ferry to Qatar — marine passenger operations at gateway scale are already licensed and running.

posture._internal: Classification per AUTHORITY-MAP-BAHRAIN.md §2: Dual, Enable-led. Every regulatory instrument found (registration, master licence, navigation licence, port/jetty licensing) is an MTT instrument; no evidence MTT operates vessels itself — hence enum enable_dominant (affects order/emphasis only; both tracks render). Never framed as replacing the water-taxi service, the ferry, or any existing operator — additive-tier language throughout.

pillars: Zero-emission electric foiling — in line with the Kingdom's net-zero 2060 target and its interim 2035 reduction, stated at COP26.
Minimal wake foilborne and near-silent at speed — marina, harbour and protected-island purposes served by design, measurable on request.
Visitor economy and quality of life: fifteen million visitors connected to the water, and commute time returned on island corridors the road network serves the long way around.

copy.headline: Bahrain writes its water rules through licences, not posted limits.
copy.framing: Navigation conduct in the Kingdom's waters is set through ministry licence conditions and Coast Guard notices, purposed for safety and security. A foiling, electric vessel serves the purposes marina and harbour rules exist for — wake, wash, noise — by design.
copy.ask: Our ask: measure us. Set each corridor's operating conditions through the licensing process that already exists — and let independently measured wake and noise define the envelope, route by route.

expander.title: What licence conditions unlock
body: The ports and marine navigation law places every port, harbour, pier and private jetty under one ministry, which licenses operators and sets the conditions they sail under. A corridor's operating envelope is therefore a licensing conversation, not a rule change.

Planning on this page is deliberately conservative: displacement speeds in marinas, channels and harbour limits, service speed only on open water, and a 06:00–18:00 modeled service day. Anything better than that basis is treated as upside — never assumed in a rendered time.

navier_intro.title: Meet the vessel

copy.headline: Zero-emission. Near-silent. Almost no wake.
copy.subline: Navier is a U.S. builder of electric hydrofoil vessels — the traits that matter for harbour rules and harbour neighbors are built into the hull, not bolted on.
copy.body: The N45 Explorer carries 30 passengers at a foilborne cruise speed of about 30 knots, lifted clear of the water for a smooth, wake-free ride. The smaller N30 Quanta carries 8. Foiling cuts energy use by up to ~90% versus a conventional planing hull, and both vessels run near-silent on electric power.

reference.title: Reference

copy.intro: Bahrain's water-transport landscape is compact and clearly mandated. We seek conversations — nothing here implies approval, endorsement, or commitment by any body named.

bodies.role: The anchor authority. Its Ports and Maritime Affairs arm regulates every port, harbour, pier and private jetty, licenses operators, registers vessels under 150 gross tonnes, and issues master and navigation licences — the single licensing home for routes, vessels and landings.
Licenses and regulates tourism businesses and runs destination promotion — the licensing home for the experience layer, and steward of a fifteen-million-visitor economy.

Controls maritime movement notices, equipment approvals and security restrictions in territorial waters. Schedule design absorbs its notices — including the evening-hours authorization this page's modeled service day respects.
Steward of the Kingdom's net-zero 2060 commitment and of protected areas — the environmental reference point for operations near the Hawar Islands.
